seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I explained to him my idea in coming here two months ago. I cabled him from here. And he has not sent even the royalties due! I am tired going up the staircase of MM Cook & Son to find out if the other member of the trinity has done what I asked him to do. But the biggesthearted man in the U.S. (according to Mr JB Yeats) has given no sign of life.

The police want fees for sojourns which I can’t pay. My concierge and Giorgio’s concierge want tips which I can’t give. Matters cannot continue like this. If no merchant of jalap or government spy comes to the rescue I shall have to put the MS of Circe aside. I spoke to an American about a position in a transport agency. I could probably get it but if I asked them for a month’s salary in advance they would probably not engage me – and the 1 September is too far off. Doles of £5 and 5/- ( uso Pinker ) are of no use. They relieve tension for a few days and just when I am getting into my stride again some other mongrel runs between my legs. I have already lost a month. If there is no hope of what I suggest please let me know at once and I shall either do as above or try to return to Trieste. I want only facilities to finish Ulysses . After that I agree to do any kind of manual labour.

I hope Mr Rodker was not bored by me as you certainly must have been. I made an attempt to haul myself out of the swamp while he was here. Don’t bother him about my affairs and don’t dream of asking him for money or of sending any of your own because I will send it back. I am sure you like my correspondence. But here I am houseless and wandering with a sixteen year old son, a daughter and a wife and with no prospect of any kind in front of me. If you and he had been my guests in Trieste (of prewar) or even in Zurich it would have been another matter.

div.note: This letter fragment was probably written in the latter part of July 1920, after Pound returned to London from Paris on 21 July (LIII 9). The reference to John Rodker in the final paragraph may relate to the visit he and his wife paid to JJ on 27 July 1920, though JJ may also have met Rodker in Paris earlier in July, probably with Pound. (For the suggestion that JJ first met Rodker before Pound’s departure from Paris on 21 July, see Lawrence Rainey, Institutions of Modernism: Literary Elites and Public Culture [New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, 1998], 46.)

Presumably JJ’s American publisher, B.W. Huebsch (1876-1964), from whom JJ was hoping to receive royalties due on published books and an advance on royalties for the book version of Ulysses, which JJ’s literary agent J.B. Pinker was trying to negotiate at this time. Pound saw no chance of “Huebsch paying £££ advance on mss. he hadn’t seen” (Pound/Joyce 183). In the end, Huebsch would not risk publishing Ulysses without changes, and JJ would not expurgate. Ulysses as a book was first published by Shakespeare and Company in Paris in February 1922. For a fuller account of JJ’s need for royalties at this time, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes.

Thomas Cook & Son, tourist agents, had offices in Paris at 2 Place de la Madeleine, 1 Place de l’Opéra, 250 Rue de Rivoli, and 101 Avenue des Champs-Elysées (Karl Baedeker, Paris and its Environs [Leipzig: Karl Baedeker, 1924], 41). JJ used the office at Place de l’Opéra on at least one occasion (see JJ to Pound, 13 August 1920).

JJ’s trinity of lifesavers was Huebsch, J.B. Pinker, and the New York lawyer John Quinn – whom JJ referred to collectively as “Huebsch, Pinker, Quinn and Co” (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920). Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, had agreed to purchase JJ’s Ulysses manuscript and had cabled JJ an advance of 3,000 lire or $153.85 on 5 February 1920. On 15 August 1920 he sent another payment of 3,400 francs or $250, with an additional sum of 1,400 francs in the fall of 1920 (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 237, 241-42, 245-46, 254, 258). For a fuller account, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

Pound had written JJ on 19 April 1917 that John Quinn was “the busiest man in America, or one of the busiest, and as old father J.B. Yeats wrote long ago ‘the biggest hearted and most irascible.’ He isn’t really irascible, but impetuous” (Pound/Joyce 110). John Butler Yeats (1839-1922) was a noted Irish artist, letter writer, and the father of the poet William Butler Yeats (1865-1939). Several of his portraits are held by the National Gallery of Ireland, including one of his son William.

The Paris prefecture of police issued permis de séjour (permits of sojourn) to foreigners for temporary visits lasting longer than a certain number of days. Pound complained that the prefecture’s rules and other requirements for visiting foreigners, especially Americans, were threatening the interests of “the Franco-American alliance” and penalized people “for having a nationality” (“Oh, Those Passports,” New York Herald [Paris] [22 July 1920].) For some time, Pound had been complaining about passport, visa, and other restrictions on cross-border travel.
JJ’s son Giorgio had to stay at a hotel early in the family’s stay in Paris (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes).

Jalap is “a herbal purgative derived from a vine in Mexico that would have been imported by colonizers to Africa primarily for use as a vermifuge to expel intestinal worms” (James Ramey, “Joycean Lice and the Life of Art,” College Literature, vol. 39, no. 1 [Winter 2012]: 43). In the first episode of Ulysses, Buck Mulligan tells Stephen Dedalus that the father of Haines – the affluent young Englishman who is staying with them at the tower – “made his tin by selling jalap to Zulus or some bloody swindle or other” (U 1.156-57).
At this time, JJ was working on “Circe,” the fifteenth and longest episode of Ulysses. For a fuller account of “Circe,” see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1920, notes.

1 September was probably the date on which JJ would receive an interest payment from a £5,000 trust fund in war loan securities that Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961) had settled on him in 1919. In late August 1920, Weaver informed him that she was increasing that original gift by another £2,000 (LIII 17). Mary Reynolds describes later increases: “in 1921 another £1,500; in 1923, when [Weaver] received an inheritance, yet another gift of £12,000; and in 1924 a final transfer of £550. (Joyce in a letter to Sylvia Beach in 1923 put the ‘total sum made over to me by her’ at £21,000 …). The money, moreover, was invested – at least initially – in securities that would be tax-free to persons not residing in England” (Mary T. Reynolds, “Joyce and Miss Weaver,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 19, no. 4 [Summer 1982]: 384). For further details, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes.

“uso Pinker” is probably an Italian phrase meaning something like “in the manner of Pinker” or “as is Pinker’s custom” – that is, the custom or habit of JJ’s literary agent of sending dribs and drabs of money.

John Rodker (1894-1955), English writer, poet, and publisher, was a contributor to the New York magazine The Little Review and succeeded Pound as its foreign editor in 1919. In the January 1919 number, Rodker published “‘Exiles’: A Discussion of James Joyce’s Play” (20-22). Also in 1919, he started the short-lived Ovid Press, an artisanal hand press and publishing firm in London which issued, among other modernist writings, a limited first edition of Pound’s Hugh Selwyn Mauberley in June 1920. In Paris, Rodker may have met JJ initially, with Pound, prior to 21 July 1920 (see Rainey, Institutions of Modernism, 46). Then, he and his wife, the British modernist writer Mary Butts (1890-1937), arrived at JJ’s apartment on Giorgio Joyce’s birthday, 27 July 1920, to find JJ “sitting gloomily silent,” listless with fatigue and financial worry. The Rodkers cheered him up by taking the “whole vagabond family” out to dinner, as JJ told Pound on 31 July 1920 (LIII 12). Pound wrote JJ that far from being bored, “Rodker was delighted to see you [and] offers to give an imprint to Ulysses if the Egoist will provide the £ for the actual printing somewhere else, which may possibly be a solution” (Pound/Joyce 183-84). Although Rodker had initially hoped to be the sole initial publisher of Ulysses in some format, this plan did not come to fruition (Rainey, Institutions of Modernism, 46-47). Instead, Ulysses was first issued as a book in February 1922 in Paris by Sylvia Beach’s Shakespeare and Company, and then in October 1922 by the Egoist Press of London, assisted by Rodker who rented a room in Paris to serve as an office from which he dispatched copies – printed in France to avoid the squeamishness of English printers – to purchasers in America, Britain, and elsewhere (Ellmann, JJ 505-06 n.†). The edition’s title page states: “PUBLISHED FOR THE | EGOIST PRESS, LONDON | BY JOHN RODKER, PARIS | 1922.”

Despite JJ’s melodramatic claim of being “houseless,” he and his family were installed by 15 July in a small flat at 5 rue de l’Assomption in Passy for three months on a rent-free basis (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes). JJ had known of the promised Passy flat at least as early as 12 July (LI 142; LIII 8) and perhaps even earlier, since its owners had described the offer to Pound on 9 July (Ludmila Bloch­Savitzky and Marcel Bloch to Pound [9 July 1920], James Joyce Collection, The Poetry Collection, University at Buffalo).
JJ and Nora Barnacle’s son Giorgio (1905-1976) turned fifteen, not sixteen, on 27 July 1920. Their daughter Lucia (1907-1982) turned thirteen on 26 July.
